books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, Democracy in America by Alexis de Tocqueville

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835, 1840)

stimulus.text: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835): “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions.” In a later volume (1840) he wrote: “Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive.”
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835) and vol. 2 (1840), Henry Reeve translation. Verbatim quotations verified against the Project Gutenberg text (eBook 815).

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Tocqueville's picture of a democratic society of equals sits uneasily with which fact about America in the 1830s?

options.text: Most Americans still farmed for a living on family farms
options.misconception: Farming was still the most common livelihood, but that does not contradict equality of conditions the way slavery and women's exclusion do.

options.text: Enslaved people were held as property, and women could not vote
The Erie Canal had linked New York to the Great Lakes
options.misconception: The canal spread commerce; it does not clash with Tocqueville's claim about equality.

options.text: Newspapers and magazines were widely read
options.misconception: A reading public fits Tocqueville's picture; it does not sit uneasily with it.

rationales.A: Most Americans farming does not contradict equality of conditions; farmers were the equals Tocqueville had in mind.
rationales.B: Tocqueville's equality described free white men. Enslaved people were property, not equals, and women could not vote, so his fundamental fact stopped at the edge of those two groups.
rationales.C: The canal is a triumph of the market revolution. It spreads the commerce Tocqueville's equals traded in; it does not contradict them.
rationales.D: Wide reading suits a democratic society. It supports Tocqueville's picture rather than sitting uneasily with it.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who his equals are. Tocqueville writes about free citizens forming associations and voting.
2. Ask who is missing. Enslaved people were property, and women had no vote.
3. Name the limit. His equality stopped at the edge of those two groups.
Background: Cotton made the South more committed to enslaved labor, while Northern free labor and Southern slavery grew further apart.
Remember: a claim about everyone deserves a check on who it leaves out.
